messages.subject: Dispersal Events_results
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone!

I am working with dispersal events matrices, considering different time slices and 6 regions.
I realized that, for all regions, the number of dispersal events increased a lot in the last period (towards to the present). See the attached figure. However, in my distance matrices, I did not consider any connection among regions in the last millions of years. So, I would expect a decrease in dispersal events in the present.

Anyone would know how to explain that? Maybe if there is a high similarity of species among all regions (i.e., high dispersal events in the past), it could cause the extremely high dispersal events in the present time. What do you think?

Thanks in advance!
Fernanda

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Dispersal Events_results
messages.body_plain:
> Hi Fernanda,
>
> A few quick thoughts:
>

> On Fri, Apr 3, 2020 at 3:59 AM Fernanda Cassemiro <fernanda...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi everyone!
> >
> > I am working with dispersal events matrices, considering different time slices and 6 regions.
> > I realized that, for all regions, the number of dispersal events increased a lot in the last period (towards to the present). See the attached figure. However, in my distance matrices, I did not consider any connection among regions in the last millions of years. So, I would expect a decrease in dispersal events in the present.
> >
> > Anyone would know how to explain that? Maybe if there is a high similarity of species among all regions (i.e., high dispersal events in the past), it could cause the extremely high dispersal events in the present time. What do you think?
>

> Unless you literally set the manual_dispersal_multiplier matrix to have "0" between all regions for the last few million years, then dispersal is possible during that time.
>
> A few things will affect the number of dispersals observed:
>
> 1. All (living) phylogenies have more branches and more branch-length towards the present than they have anywhere else. So, the dispersal counts are likely to be highest towards the tips (just like there will be more recorded nodes for speciation events, etc.)
>
> 2. If you did estimate lots of dispersal deep in the tree, then this could push the d and/or j parameter to high values, and these high parameters could "force" some dispersal events even for recent clades where (say) parsimony would say none occurred. Combined with #1, this might produce a spike like you see.
>
> 3. Also, if you have some tips with widespread ranges (e.g. range ABC instead of A), then one common way the models would explain this is by invoking a bunch of "d" events on the tip branches.
>
> My best bet, not knowing the dataset, would be a combination of #1 and #3.  Regardless, it is interesting you have a "hump" deeper back in time, that does suggest something interesting is going on.
>
> Cheers!
> Nick
>

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am working through the example script for Biogeographic stochastic mapping (http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeographical-stochastic-mapping-example-script#BSM_script_plain) and wanted to ask a question regarding the summary counts. Below is the "Summary_counts_BSMs" table
founder
a d e subset vicariance sympatry ALL_disp ana_disp all_ana all_clado total_events
means
0 0 5.7 0 3.6 4.94 9.46 5.7 5.7 5.7 18 23.7
stdevs
0 0 0.89 0 1.69 1.02 1.86 0.89 0.89 0.89 0 0.89
sums
0 0 285 0 180 247 473 285 285 285 900 1185

The values for the e parameter are all zeros, and I think these relate to for range contraction/extinction based on this figure http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#BioGeoBEARS_supermodel_graphic

However, if I look at ana_events_tables[1] and ana_events_tables[2] for example, I can see a column related to event types with e event types

selection from ana_events_tables[1]

event_time event_type event_txt
0.13524266 e KO->O
1.34103794 d K->KO
0.03030695 d O->OM
0.38716861 d KM->KMH
0.43218619 d KMH->KOMH
0.6046524 d K->KO

selection from ana_events_tables[2]

event_time event_type event_txt
1.21431375 e OM->M
1.69944131 e KO->O
0.90854886 d O->KO
0.08155875 d O->OM
0.30394174 d OM->OMH
0.21643962 d O->KO

And on the corresponding trees, I can see examples of e events. I have attached screen grabs of the first two trees with crude annotation.

Am I correct in assuming the the e parameter is being modeled in the BSM analysis? If it is, why are the summary numbers all zeros?

I hope this all makes sense and apologies if I have misunderstood something here.

Best wishes
Ollie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick!

Thanks very much for the prompt reply.

My phylogeny has more branch-length towards the present, and many tips with widespread ranges as well. The hump in the past is strictly correlated to important geological events in South America, which connected some regions in the past and boosted the dispersal. It's a really cool result.

Is there a way to solve this issue? Maybe if I calculate relative numbers of dispersal events by dividing absolute numbers by the total length of all branches within each time bin, it could minimize the peak of dispersal in the present.

Best,
Fernanda

messages.body_plain:

Sorry if I have missed something very obvious here, but I cannot find the information along the documentation.

Thanks a lot!
Andrea

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] summarise stochastic mapps - consensus tree
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrea,

Do you mean summarizing across multiple different topologies, or summarizing multiple stochastic maps on the same topology?  The 2nd option is basically what you get with a standard ML ancestral states estimate, since the average of all of the stochastic maps will converge on the ancestral states estimate.   The former is very challenging to imagine what is even meant -- it would be coherent to count events per-time-bin across multiple trees, or something like that, but very difficult to imagine what a consensus depiction on a single summary tree would look like.

The problem is similar to the problem with "Bayes-DIVA", "Bayes-Lagrange", etc.,

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/biogeobears/M8zw8Kidseo

...but even more complex!

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] Re: summarise stochastic mapps - consensus tree
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrea!

It is imaginable that one could calculate, from a bunch of BSMs, the average time along a branch where a particular "d" event occurred. Then you could "paint" the branch to transition at that point.  Although -- my gut feeling is that anagenetic events are usually pretty uniformly distributed in time along a branch (I haven't dug into it).

Or, conceivably, one could have some kind of graduated color scheme indicating increasing probability of the transition having occurred on a branch. I believe phytools has this for standard characters.  It is possible to convert BioGeoBEARS BSMs into phytools format (meaning I wrote a script at some point, I could find it if needed), and then I guess one could try applying phytools's paintings and summaries, but I'm not sure this would yield much that would be useful as a visualization, given that the biogeography analyses often have hundreds of states/colors, while the phytools ones are typically 2 or 3 states/colors.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hello again,

Please excuse my long-winded code, but I had a go at counting the number of anagenetic dispersal events in the short term.

# create empty matrix with 3 columns and rows equal the number of BSM iterations
my_ana_events_counts <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(ana_events_tables), ncol = 3)

# set column names in matrix
colnames(my_ana_events_counts) <- c("d","e","all")

# for loop iterates through ana_events_tables and counts the number of d, e and all events
for (i in 1:length(ana_events_tables)) {
  ana_events_table <- ana_events_tables[i]
  event_type <- as.data.frame(ana_events_table)[,"event_type"]
  my_ana_events_counts[i,1] <- sum(event_type == "d")
  my_ana_events_counts[i,2] <- sum(event_type == "e")
  my_ana_events_counts[i,3] <- length(event_type)
}

# check output
head(my_ana_events_counts)

# function to calculate mean, sd and total
my_summary_counts <- function(x) {
  print(c(signif(mean(x), 2),
          signif(sd(x), 2),
          sum(x)))
}

# calculate mean, sd and total for d, e and all
d <- my_summary_counts(my_ana_events_counts[,"d"])
e <- my_summary_counts(my_ana_events_counts[,"e"] )
all <- my_summary_counts(my_ana_events_counts[,"all"])

# create dataframe
df <- data.frame(d, e, all)
row.names(df) <- c("mean", "sd", "total")

df

Working on the same example dataset, the df output looks like this

d e all
mean 5.7 1.6 7.3
sd 0.89 1.1 1.7
total 285 78 363

Hopefully this makes sense

Best wishes
Ollie
